name: Open Source Maintainers
blurb: The people keeping critical AI infrastructure alive.

members.hook: O'Reilly has spent four decades doing the same thing under different names: spotting a technology shift before the industry has language for it, then naming it. 'Open source' and 'Web 2.0' both trace to conferences he convened, and his publishing house has been the technical-literacy backbone for the programmers who built the modern internet, and now AI.
members.name: Tim O'Reilly
members.moniker: Publisher Who Named Web 2.0 and the Open Source Movement

reading.body:
Tim O'Reilly's primary contribution to AI infrastructure is not code but language: by naming and convening around technology shifts, he shaped which ideas programmers organized around and which tools they built together.

The pattern across four decades is consistent. A shift arrives before the industry has shared vocabulary for it, and O'Reilly supplies that vocabulary through conferences and publishing. The programmers who absorbed that framing then built the infrastructure the next era runs on. That process matters for AI specifically because open-source tooling, trained and maintained by communities with shared conceptual language, sits directly beneath the compute that runs modern models.

What this data does not cover is the technical work of the maintainers who write and sustain that code day to day. The dataset contains one person, described in terms of naming and publishing rather than software contribution. It establishes context for the open-source ecosystem rather than mapping its active maintenance layer.
